content: The analysis of three British birth cohorts (1946, 1958, and 1970) revealed that obesity in adulthood, when combined with any pattern of overweight during earlier life stages, was associated with a significantly increased risk of developing type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) compared to individuals who were never overweight. However, being overweight exclusively during childhood or adolescence did not increase the odds of developing T2DM when compared to those who were never overweight. A pooled analysis of cohorts from four high-income countries (Bogalusa, Muscatine, Young Finn, and CDAH studies) involving 6,328 participants demonstrated that childhood overweight or obesity was a predictor of T2DM in all cohorts except the CDAH study. The relative risk (RR) of T2DM among individuals who were overweight or obese during childhood but non-obese as adults (Group II) was comparable to those with consistently normal BMI. This risk was significantly lower than that observed in individuals who were consistently obese or became obese as adults (Groups III and IV). Ten studies (eight cohorts) examined the relationship between childhood anthropometric measures (such as BMI, weight, and height) and the development of T2DM later in life. These studies reported a range of outcomes, including prevalence, risk (odds ratio), and mortality. Six of the studies were conducted in high-income countries, while one was based in a lowand middle-income country, India (New Delhi Birth Cohort). Two studies found that higher BMI between ages 4 and 18 was associated with an increased risk of developing diabetes in adulthood, although one of these studies did not have an adequate follow-up period. The New Delhi Birth Cohort study found that lower BMI at age 2 and higher BMI at age 14 were associated with an increased risk of diabetes in adulthood. Another study from the same cohort reported that individuals with the lowest BMI at age 2 and the highest BMI at age 12 had a higher prevalence of diabetes. In the 1958 British Birth Cohort, BMI gain was divided into tertiles, and the risk of diabetes was significantly higher in the upper tertile compared to the lower tertile. Two studies from the New Delhi Birth Cohort also found that rapid increases in BMI during childhood and adolescence were associated with a higher risk of diabetes later in life. A study on the Norwegian population categorized adolescent BMI into quartiles and found that individuals in the highest two quartiles had the highest risk of mortality due to diabetes mellitus in adulthood. The Hertfordshire Cohort Study reported that the highest prevalence of diabetes was observed in individuals with the lowest weight at age 1. Similarly, the 1946 British Birth Cohort demonstrated that lower weight at age 2 was associated with an increased risk of developing T2DM in adulthood. Another study from the New Delhi Birth Cohort found that greater weight gain between early childhood and adulthood increased the risk of developing diabetes. Five studies (four cohorts) investigated the relationship between childhood BMI, height, and weight with HOMA-IR (a measure of insulin resistance) levels in adulthood. Three cohorts from developed countries and one from a lowand middle-income country were included. Two studies from the Vulnerable Windows Birth Cohort found a positive association between increases in height, weight, and BMI with HOMA-IR in adolescence. However, another study from the same cohort did not find a significant association between childhood and adolescent BMI and the development of insulin resistance in adulthood. The New Delhi Birth Cohort study reported that changes in conditional BMI and weight from age 2 to adulthood were significantly associated with the development of insulin resistance in adulthood. One study from the NHLBI reported that the development of impaired glucose tolerance was associated with baseline BMI in Black girls and the rate of BMI increase in White girls. However, childhood BMI was inversely related to HOMA-IR in adulthood as reported by the Boyd Orr Cohort. A study from the Northern Finland Birth Cohort 1966 found that the risk of high fasting glucose levels in adulthood was significant only in the highest BMI percentile during infancy. The Bogalusa Heart Study found a significant association between adolescent weight status and BMI changes with adult glucose levels. In contrast, the New Delhi Birth Cohort demonstrated that changes in conditional BMI from age 11 to adulthood were significantly associated with high glucose levels in adulthood. Height was also studied as an exposure variable for its association with glucose levels. Studies from the Vulnerable Windows Cohort and the Northern Finland Birth Cohort 1966 found no association between increased risk of high glucose levels in adolescence and adulthood with height at birth. However, one study from the Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children reported no increase in the odds of developing high glucose levels in late adolescence with an increase in waist circumference during childhood. The Northern Finland Birth Cohort 1966 also studied the association of age at adiposity rebound with adulthood glucose levels and found no significant relationship. A pooled analysis from five lowand middle-income countries (Brazil, Guatemala, New Delhi, Philippines, and South Africa) showed that higher conditional weights (CW) were associated with increased blood pressure and odds of prehypertension/hypertension, with coefficients proportional to the contribution of each CW to adult BMI. However, when adjusted for adult height and BMI, no childhood CW was associated with adult blood pressure.
